newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Resistance and talks halt Afghan rebel advance.
newsitem.headline: Resistance and talks halt Afghan rebel advance.

text.p: After a week of victories, a rebel advance in eastern Afghanistan has been halted by stiff resistance from government forces, Afghan sources in Pakistan said on Saturday.
The rebel wave has been checked east of the capital Kabul and in Kunar province, they added.

Intense fighting between forces loyal to President Burhanuddin Rabbani and the rebel Taleban Islamic militia raged for the third day on Saturday about 30 km (18 miles) east of the strategic town of Sarobi, Taleban sources said.
Taleban, which controls more than half of Afghanistan, including key land routes, is trying to topple Rabbani's government and enforce a strict Islamic order throughout the war-shattered country.

There was no report on any progress in the latest fighting either by government forces or the Taleban, which has pushed east in the past week and seized the adjoining strategic provinces of Nangarhar and Laghman in its drive to control maximum territory before any internationally-brokered peace deal.

In Kunar, which borders Pakistan, the invading militia and the pro-government administration continued peace talks for the second day on Saturday, Taleban sources in the northwestern Pakistani town of Peshawar said.
On Friday, a Taleban source in Peshawar said the militia had seized Kunar, but other Afghan sources denied the claim.
"Kunar will come under Taleban control as the local administration does not want to fight," a Taleban spokesman in Peshawar said on Saturday. "Our talks are continuing."

A Pakistan-based Afghan news service said about 300 elders and local commanders held a meeting at the Kunar province capital of Asadabad on Friday to discuss whether to surrender or put up a fight. But no decision had been announced.
Both sides are using heavy weapons, including tanks, in the battle for Sarobi, 60 km (37 miles) from Kabul, the Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) said.
Taleban captured Nangarhar and Laghman provinces without a fight on Wednesday and Friday respectively after the defenders either fled or surrendered.

But AIP said Sarobi is defended by more battle-hardened troops, including those of the Shura-i-Nazar group of top government military commander Ahmad Shah Masood, famed for his exploits against Soviet occupation in the 1980s.

Afghan government officials in Kabul said on Friday government troops had pulled back from Laghman to establish defensive belts in a plateau overlooking Sarobi, which has been a stronghold of the Hezb-i-Islami party of Prime Minister Gulbuddin Hekmatyar.
President Rabbani, in a speech in Kabul on Thursday, vowed to fight to the last and called Taleban "enemies of Afghanistan."
